title: Ten Questions Concerning Well-Being in the Built Environment
central_proposition: The promotion of well-being in the built environment necessitates a departure from conventional agendas and the integration of diverse new competencies to address the multifaceted physical, physiological, and psychological needs of occupants.

concept_definitions.name: Well-being
concept_definitions.definition: A broader, more holistic approach reflecting a wide construct of physical, physiological, social, economic, and psychological aspects, combining hedonic (feeling good) and eudemonic (functioning well) dimensions, moving beyond accepted definitions of comfort and health.

concept_definitions.name: Comfort
concept_definitions.definition: The condition of mind that expresses satisfaction with the environment, assessed by subjective evaluation.

concept_definitions.name: Health
concept_definitions.definition: A state of complete physical, mental, and social well-being, not merely the absence of disease or infirmity.

concept_definitions.name: Health Performance Indicators (HPIs)
concept_definitions.definition: A framework that puts health and human performance at the center of business decision-making, bringing concepts from health science to business executives.

argument_structure: The paper is structured around ten questions and answers, offering expert perspectives on principles and strategies for well-being in the built environment. It progresses from general design considerations (Q1-Q2) to specific indoor environmental quality domains (Q3-Q6), then to monitoring and organizational strategies (Q7-Q8), and finally to future research and practice integration (Q9-Q10). This structure builds towards a new framework emphasizing interdisciplinary competencies and a shift from risk-avoidance to positive outcomes.
mechanism_or_causal_logic: The built environment influences occupant well-being through multifaceted, dynamic, and individual-specific physical, physiological, and psychological factors. Key mechanisms include multi-sensory variability and personal control, which allow individuals to tune their experiences and move beyond static comfort. The paper argues for an 'integrated analysis approach' that considers complex interactions between environmental stressors and diverse human responses, moving from preventing ill-being to actively promoting positive stimuli and 'value-adding' experiences.

findings.antecedent: Opportunities of exposure to a dynamic natural ecosystem (rich and mutable stimuli)
findings.consequent: Tune the pulse of human lives (well-being)
findings.mechanism: Humans have evolved in connection to dynamic natural ecosystems, which consistently served as key drivers for their physiological and psychological rhythms.
findings.quote: From an evolutionary perspective, humans have grown in connec- tion to a dynamic natural ecosystem; opportunities of exposure to its rich and mutable stimuli have consistently represented key drivers to tune the pulse of their lives [28].

findings.antecedent: Built environments providing opportunities for multi-sensory variability and personal control
findings.consequent: Occupant well-being (health, cognitive performance, experiential delight)
findings.mechanism: Allows individuals to tune their experiences to their needs, moving beyond static comfort and engaging multiple sensory channels dynamically.
findings.quote: The premise is that one of the keys to moving upward on this pyramid is sensory variability, where the environmental conditions we encounter vary in subtle ways, either dynamically throughout the day, or spatially across the different places we inhabit. This can have benefits for our health, cognitive performance, and overall experiential delight.

findings.antecedent: Design that supports alliesthesia (physiological basis for thermal delight)
findings.consequent: Thermal delight and well-being
findings.mechanism: Hedonic sensations of pleasure arise from the dynamic component of thermoreceptors in the skin, implying that variability, rather than static conditions, is key.
findings.quote: For thermal variability, in particular, there is increasing evidence for the concept of alliesthesia - the physiological basis for thermal delight, which also has analogies to other senses as well [40,56,57]. The premise is that hedonic sensations of 'pleasure' come from the dynamic component of thermoreceptors in our skin [58-60].

findings.antecedent: Environmental conditions that vary in subtle ways (dynamically or spatially)
findings.consequent: Health, cognitive performance, and overall experiential delight
findings.mechanism: Sensory variability moves beyond static comfort, providing benefits across multiple domains.
findings.quote: The premise is that one of the keys to moving upward on this pyramid is sensory variability, where the environmental conditions we encounter vary in subtle ways, either dynamically throughout the day, or spatially across the different places we inhabit. This can have benefits for our health, cognitive performance, and overall experiential delight.

findings.antecedent: Exposure to mildly cold or warm environments outside of the standard comfort temperature range
findings.consequent: Metabolism and energy expenditure
findings.mechanism: Helps tackle obesity and influences glucose metabolism and insulin sensitivity.
findings.quote: As one example of health benefits, exposure to mildly cold or warm environments outside of the standard comfort temperature range was found to increase metabolism and energy expenditure, which can help to tackle obesity [50].

findings.antecedent: Variable temperatures (compared to constant mean values)
findings.consequent: Symptoms of drowsiness and difficulty in concentration
findings.mechanism: Implies cognitive engagement or reduced monotony, preventing cognitive fatigue.
findings.quote: a study exposed subjects to both constant and sawtooth temperatures with similar mean values, and found that the variable temperatures reduced symptoms of drowsiness and difficulty in con- centration [51].

findings.antecedent: Daily patterns of exposure to light and dark (timing, intensity, duration, spectral content, history, geometry)
findings.consequent: Circadian rhythms, sleep cycles, memory formation, immune response, growth, development, and metabolic health
findings.mechanism: Light acts on the eye's circadian photoreceptors, influencing various physiological processes.
findings.quote: Daily patterns of exposure to light and dark are key determinants of our circadian rhythms, influencing sleep cycles, memory formation, immune response, growth, development, and metabolic health.

findings.antecedent: Exposure to blue portion of the visible spectrum at night (indoors or outdoors)
findings.consequent: Sleep disruption
findings.mechanism: Suppression of the hormone melatonin, which regulates sleep.
findings.quote: it is now established that exposure to this blue portion of the visible spectrum at night, whether indoors or outdoors, can cause sleep disruption via suppression of the hormone melatonin [66].

findings.antecedent: Naturally daylit spaces (locally appropriate circadian stimulus)
findings.consequent: Healthiest lighting scenarios
findings.mechanism: Mimics Earth's natural cycle of bright days and dark nights, which humans evolved under.
findings.quote: Given this, the easiest way to achieve locally appropriate circadian stimulus inside of buildings is via naturally daylit spaces.

findings.antecedent: Attractive window views of the outdoors
findings.consequent: Occupants' circadian well-being
findings.mechanism: Offers significantly more circadian stimulus to the eye than ambient daylight alone.
findings.quote: buildings can also support occupants' circadian well-being via attractive window views of the outdoors, which can offer about an order of magnitude more circadian stimulus to 'the eye of the beholder' than even ambient daylight inside of a space [39].

findings.antecedent: Access to window views
findings.consequent: General eye health
findings.mechanism: Provides motivation for occupants to frequently refocus their eyes, maintaining muscle tone and lubrication.
findings.quote: Access to window views is also important for general eye health... An interesting window view provides the motivation to do exactly that.

findings.antecedent: Glare-free window views
findings.consequent: Educational progress, processing speed, sleep, working memory capacity
findings.mechanism: Provides information, stimulation, and relaxation, enhancing cognitive functions and restorative processes.
findings.quote: Glare-free window views have been positively associated with many objectively measurable outcomes, including greater educational prog- ress in schools [69,70], faster processing speed by call centre workers [71], and, in office settings, improved sleep [72], greater working memory capacity, and fewer reports of fatigue and other health complaints [71].

findings.antecedent: Visual environment (sources of light, reflections, shadows, sparkle, relative brightness, interest in visual scene)
findings.consequent: Mood, visual comfort, cognitive performance, circadian well-being
findings.mechanism: Holistic consideration of all visual elements, including dynamic contributions and occupant focus, influences perception and physiological responses.
findings.quote: The visual environment includes not just the sources of light... but rather everything that we look at. Reflections off of surfaces also determine the colour and distribution of light within a space. Shadows and sparkle can influence mood. For the visual comfort of occupants, relative brightness is more important than absolute levels of illumina- tion, and interest in a visual scene is often much more important than glare [74].
findings.empirical_support_cited: Cited [74] for interest in visual scene.

findings.antecedent: Beautiful luminous environment
findings.consequent: Aesthetic pleasure and motivation
findings.mechanism: Provides positive emotional and motivational responses through aesthetic appreciation.
findings.quote: A beautiful luminous environment importantly provides aesthetic pleasure and motivation for people.

findings.antecedent: Thermal discomfort
findings.consequent: Building-related symptoms and reduced performance
findings.mechanism: Physiological stress and cognitive distraction caused by uncomfortable thermal conditions.
findings.quote: Nevertheless, thermal discomfort may cause building-related symptoms and reduce performance [79,80].

findings.antecedent: Personal comfort system (PCS) with higher levels of personal control
findings.consequent: Thermal comfort and well-being
findings.mechanism: Allows individuals to adjust their immediate surroundings to their preferences, enhancing their sense of control and physiological comfort.
findings.quote: To date, the main technology that showed in labs and field studies the potential to provide a high level of thermal comfort is the use of a personal comfort system (PCS)... The higher the level of personal control, the higher the classification, the higher the thermal comfort.

findings.antecedent: Personal comfort models (PCM) that predict individuals' thermal comfort responses
findings.consequent: Thermal satisfaction and well-being
findings.mechanism: PCMs adapt to individual data (environmental measurements, occupant feedback, behavior, physiological parameters) to provide personalized control, moving beyond average population models.
findings.quote: A modelling strategy that showed higher accuracy is named personal comfort models (PCM). PCM is a new approach to thermal comfort modelling that predicts individuals' thermal comfort responses, instead of the average response of a large population [87]. Personal comfort models can be based on environmental measurements (e.g., air tem- perature, location, relative humidity), occupant feedback (e.g., online voting), occupant behaviour (e.g., thermostat set points) and physio- logical parameters (e.g., skin temperature, heart rate) to train a model that is valid for a specific person or group [88]. PCMs have the ability to adapt as new data are introduced in the model [87].

findings.antecedent: Appropriate acoustic design (varying room volume, shape, materials, construction, control strategies for noise)
findings.consequent: Occupants maintain healthy hearing, perform as expected, and participate comfortably
findings.mechanism: Reduces negative effects of noise and unwanted sound, allowing for optimal auditory function and cognitive performance.
findings.quote: Past research in architectural acoustics has focused primarily on addressing the lower parts of the pyramid, gathering data that confirm how appropriate acoustic design can reduce negative effects on occu- pants.

findings.antecedent: Lower background noise levels, lower reverberation times, and wall/door/window constructions with high sound transmission loss (in classrooms)
findings.consequent: Speech comprehension
findings.mechanism: Reduces auditory interference and improves signal-to-noise ratio for verbal communication.
findings.quote: Classrooms are used primarily for teaching and learning, so optimising speech comprehension is key. This typically requires lower background noise levels, lower reverberation times, and wall/door/ window constructions with high sound transmission loss [91].

findings.antecedent: Chronic noise exposure
findings.consequent: Stress, sleep disturbance, hypertension, cardiovascular diseases, cognitive impairment, tinnitus, hearing loss
findings.mechanism: Physiological and psychological responses to unwanted sound, leading to allostatic load and disruption of cognitive and restorative processes.
findings.quote: Conversely, evidence of the severe non-auditory health effects of envi- ronmental noise (e.g., from roads, railways, air traffic, etc.) is growing [98]; chronic exposure can lead to stress, sleep disturbance, hyperten- sion, cardiovascular diseases (e.g., ischaemic heart diseases, stroke), cognitive impairment (especially in children), etc.

findings.antecedent: Background speech from other persons (in workplaces)
findings.consequent: Ability to sustain cognitive flows, absenteeism, job satisfaction, work performance
findings.mechanism: Distraction and cognitive interference caused by unwanted auditory stimuli.
findings.quote: In the workplace, distractions caused by noise sources in the environment, such as back- ground speech from other persons, can have negative effects on the ability to sustain cognitive flows, influencing absenteeism, job satis- faction, and work performance [99].

findings.antecedent: Soundscape that changes dynamically in time and is subjectively perceived
findings.consequent: Occupant experiences of aural settings
findings.mechanism: The built environment's conception, layout, usage, and noise sources influence how people perceive and interact with the auditory environment.
findings.quote: Better appreciation and understanding of how the soundscape changes dynamically in time and is subjectively perceived by people due to the built environment's conception, layout, usage, and noise sources, can help to better predict, design, and manage occupant experiences of aural settings.

findings.antecedent: Positively evaluated soundscapes (e.g., trickling water, birds chirping)
findings.consequent: Stress recovery and physio-psychological well-being
findings.mechanism: Restorative impact of natural or pleasant sounds on physiological and psychological states.
findings.quote: greater consideration of the multifactorial nature of sound perception, and the restorative impact of positively evaluated soundscapes on stress recovery and physio-psychological well-being – e. g., the sound of trickling water or birds chirping is also undergoing wide scientific investigation [102].

findings.antecedent: Poor indoor air quality (pollutants)
findings.consequent: Discomfort, health risks, work performance, learning, sick absence, acute health symptoms (irritation of mucous membranes, airways problems, headaches, difficulty to concentrate, fatigue, allergies, asthma)
findings.mechanism: Uptake of air pollution through breathing and skin, leading to physiological and cognitive impairments.
findings.quote: Research on indoor air quality does not leave any doubt on its importance to support well-being in buildings. Reducing levels of pol- lutants, or avoiding them indoors, leads to decreased discomfort, lower health risks, better work performance and learning [114-117]... Improving air quality can reduce the intensity and prevalence of acute health symptoms re- ported by occupants, these including irritation of mucous membranes, problems with airways, headaches, difficulty to concentrate, fatigue, allergies, asthma, etc. [124-128].

findings.antecedent: High air quality in bedrooms
findings.consequent: Quality of sleep and next-day cognitive performance
findings.mechanism: Reduced physiological stress and improved restorative processes during sleep.
findings.quote: Some studies have shown that ensuring high air quality in bedrooms results in improved quality of sleep and better next-day cognitive performance [120,121].

findings.antecedent: Reduced air temperature and humidity, increased air speed
findings.consequent: Perceived air quality
findings.mechanism: Reduced sensory irritation and improved comfort perception.
findings.quote: Positive effects on perceived air quality can be enhanced when air temperature and humidity are reduced [80] and air speed is increased [122,123].

findings.antecedent: Shift from 'pathogenesis' to 'salutogenesis' (health promotion)
findings.consequent: Change in what is monitored and measured in buildings
findings.mechanism: New definitions of health and well-being demand corresponding metrics that capture positive outcomes, not just absence of disease.
findings.quote: being replaced with ones that capture well-being and health promotion; a move from pathogenesis to salutogenesis [132,133]. This change in definition demands a corresponding change in what we monitor and measure in our buildings.

findings.antecedent: Using Health Performance Indicators (HPIs) that put health and human performance at the center of business decision-making
findings.consequent: Improved health and performance outcomes
findings.mechanism: Shifts focus from traditional KPIs to metrics that directly influence health and performance, making building performance a central HPI and driving business decisions.
findings.quote: To effectively monitor health and well-being in the built environ- ment requires us to do a better job of defining what needs to get tracked and measured. We have previously promulgated a framework for doing just this, promoting the case for a fundamental shift from using the language of KPIs to using HPIs, for Health Performance Indicators [21]. The HPI approach puts health and human performance at the centre of business decision-making [135].

findings.antecedent: Coordination between corporate functions (human resources and facilities management) and tracking HPIs
findings.consequent: Support for individual well-being and organizational performance
findings.mechanism: Ensures that individuals' needs are provided for, balancing against corporate goals, and integrating information for better decision-making.
findings.quote: Supporting individual well-being in existing buildings demands co- ordination between corporate functions for human resources and facil- ities management.

findings.antecedent: Local control (hands-on adjustments or automated systems based on user settings)
findings.consequent: Individuals experience preferred conditions, better outcomes for individuals and the organization
findings.mechanism: Allows individuals to tune their environment to their preferences, which are associated with better outcomes for well-being and productivity.
findings.quote: Thus, another element of successful building operation will be local control. This may be in the form of hands-on adjustments to conditions that are available to the user, or adjustments made by an automated system based on user settings the technology is immaterial. The important consideration is to make it possible for individuals to expe- rience conditions that they prefer, which are associated with better outcomes for both individuals and the organization (e.g. [145,146])

findings.antecedent: Complex research model that includes interactions for both the environment (situation) and the occupants (profiles), acknowledging other stressors and their integrated effects, interactions, and different needs and preferences
findings.consequent: Explanation of symptoms and complaints in specified situations
findings.mechanism: Moves beyond conventional dose-response relationships to match profiles of people with patterns of positive and negative stressors, providing a more holistic understanding.
findings.quote: There is clearly a need for a more complex research model to explain symptoms and complaints in specified (exposure) situations, acknowl- edging other stressors and their integrated effects, interactions, and different needs and preferences of the occupant: a model that includes interactions for both the environment (the situation) and the occupants (Fig. 3).

findings.antecedent: Determining patterns of stressors (physical, physiological, personal, social, environmental)
findings.consequent: Understanding well-being in different situations
findings.mechanism: Identification of factors beyond environmental parameters used in guidelines, providing a more comprehensive view of influences on well-being.
findings.quote: To be able to determine patterns of stressors of importance to people in different situations, other factors and stressors than the environ- mental parameters used in guidelines - whether of psychological, physiological, personal, social, or environmental nature – will need to be identified.

findings.antecedent: Determining profiles of people (preferences and needs of individuals, positive and negative effects)
findings.consequent: Understanding well-being in different scenarios and situations
findings.mechanism: Allows for matching individual profiles to specific stressors and environmental conditions, enabling personalized design and interventions.
findings.quote: To be able to determine profiles of people for different scenarios and situations, preferences and needs of individuals, as well as positive and negative effects, will need to be identified.

findings.antecedent: Exploring interactions at and between different levels (human and environment) over time
findings.consequent: Understanding well-being in different scenarios and situations
findings.mechanism: Reveals how the human body copes with environmental stressors and how multisensory inputs interact at the central nervous system level.
findings.quote: Possible interactions at and between different levels (human and environment) over time need to be explored for different scenarios and situations... interactions between different acoustic, olfactory, and visual stressors probably occur at the level of the central nervous system [155].

findings.antecedent: Interdisciplinary approach and metrics (for researchers), understanding value of third-party involvement (for design teams)
findings.consequent: Effective translation of scientific data to building-level interventions and improved occupant health/well-being
findings.mechanism: Overcomes challenges of discipline-specific understandings and reliance on simpler IEQ satisfaction surveys, fostering a more holistic and evidence-based practice.
findings.quote: This requires a shift in thinking for both researchers, who need to embrace interdisciplinary metrics, and design teams, who are more familiar with simpler IEQ satisfaction surveys and who may not understand the value of third-party involvement.

findings.antecedent: Ongoing dialogue between researchers and standard-setting bodies, feedback loops through building and occupant evaluations, commitment to interdisciplinary collaboration, creation of key priorities for well-being and building research
findings.consequent: Achievement of well-being goals in building practice and standards
findings.mechanism: Ensures evidence-based translation and adaptation to real-world constraints, fostering a continuous improvement cycle.
findings.quote: Ensuring ongoing dialogue between researchers and standard-setting bodies who influence building design and operations, feedback loops through both building and occupant evaluations, a commitment to interdisciplinary collaboration, and the creation of key priorities for well-being and building research that can be communicated to funding bodies, policy makers, and researchers, are some ways to achieve these goals.

testable_hypotheses_or_predictions: Patterns of stressors (physical, physiological, personal, social, environmental) can be determined for people in different situations.
Profiles of people, including their preferences and needs, as well as positive and negative effects, can be identified for different scenarios and situations.
Interactions at and between different levels (human and environment) over time can be explored for different scenarios and situations.

Combined field and laboratory studies using mixed (quantitative and qualitative) design and non-linear analysis methods can determine patterns of stressors, profiles of people, and interactions at both environment and human level, and their ranges of variation.
bridge_warrants: The paper uses Maslow's hierarchy of needs to illustrate levels of occupant experience, from basic needs to self-actualization, integrating well-being into a broader human needs framework.
It connects the physiological concept of 'alliesthesia' to thermal delight, bridging sensory physiology with architectural design for well-being.
The paper proposes a shift from traditional Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) to Health Performance Indicators (HPIs), linking health outcomes to business value and organizational management.
It aligns the promotion of well-being in the built environment with the UN Sustainable Development Goals, framing it as essential for a more sustainable future.
The paper positions well-being as the 'new green' for the building industry, expanding the conventional sustainability agenda beyond energy efficiency to include human-centric outcomes.
methodological_critiques: Conventional design drivers and criteria for high-performing and green-rated buildings have primarily focused on efficiency (energy, constructability, siting, resources, costs, environmental qualities), often failing to substantiate improved occupant experience in terms of IEQ.
Self-assessment methods and reliance on indirect and subjective metrics used to measure occupant evaluations and responses may not correspond to design and green rating objectives.
Current thermal comfort models (e.g., PMV, adaptive comfort) have low prediction accuracy for individuals and are questioned for different age groups.

Indoor environmental quality (IEQ) assessment is often based on linear single dose-response relationships for negative stressors, developed for the 'average' occupant, neglecting individual differences, various scenarios, other stressors, and complex interactions.
No simple unified and universal index has been successfully established to prescribe the levels and components of indoor air quality.
model_structure: The paper proposes a 'pyramid' of occupant experience, ranging from 'Discomfort, Deprivation' (habituability threshold) to 'Comfort, Sufficiency' (standards threshold), 'Pleasure, Well-Being' (delight, alliesthesia, sensory space, biophilia), and 'Self-actualisation' (Fig. 2). It also introduces an 'integrated analysis approach' model (Fig. 3) comprising an 'Environment model' and a 'Human model' that interact to produce 'Effects (long- & short-term)'. The 'Environment model' (Fig. 4) details 'Psycho-social stressors' and 'Physical stressors' influencing 'Situation patterns of stressors'. The 'Human model' (Fig. 5) includes 'Confounders', 'Human body and systems' (stress response mechanisms), and 'Modifiers' leading to 'Effects & responses'.
limitations: The voluntary nature of certification schemes, potential trade-offs between priorities, and theoretical/practical uncertainties hinder consistent well-being implementation.
The paper does not fully resolve the heterogeneity of semantic approaches to defining well-being.
The proposed framework is not a 'universal', all-embracing recipe invariably applicable to all well-being outcomes.
Other building types (e.g., hospitals) may require more specialized considerations, though general concepts remain pertinent.
Significant gaps remain in both evidence and practice regarding work environments that support individual and organizational goals.
Scientific advances in this field are not a cumulative process but may require a 'reconstruction of the field from its fundamentals'.

Challenges remain in addressing disconnections between different demands (e.g., financial returns, environmental preservation, personal welfare) to craft resilient, restorative, variable, controllable, and positive-stimuli environments.

theory_commitments.specific_claim: Natural environments and certain built environment features can restore directed attention and reduce mental fatigue.
Exposure to natural elements in the built environment can lead to physiological stress reduction.
An innate human tendency to connect with nature influences well-being in the built environment, suggesting the importance of biophilic design.
The built environment can provide resources for health and well-being, fostering a sense of coherence rather than focusing solely on disease prevention.
Well-being in the built environment is influenced by multiple interacting levels, from individual experiences to broader social and environmental contexts.

mechanism_chain.description: Exposure to dynamic natural ecosystems provides rich and mutable stimuli that engage involuntary attention, leading to cognitive restoration and stress reduction, which in turn enhances overall well-being.

steps.from_construct: Opportunities of exposure to a dynamic natural ecosystem (rich and mutable stimuli)

steps.to_construct: Restoration of directed attention / Reduction of cognitive fatigue

steps.from_construct: Restoration of directed attention / Reduction of cognitive fatigue
